analysis.one_liner: Bars hospitals from surprise-billing patients more than they would owe an in-network hospital.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with 33 cosponsors, never received a hearing or a vote and died in House committees.
analysis.plain_summary: When patients go to a hospital, they can be treated by doctors or departments that are outside their insurance network and then billed for the difference — a "surprise bill." This bill, a condition of Medicare participation for hospitals, would have required hospitals to tell patients in advance when any provider is out of network and what the extra charge would be. Patients could not be charged more than the extra estimated amount unless they signed a consent form at least 24 hours ahead, and for emergency or same-day care, they could never be charged more than an in-network co-pay.
analysis.who_benefits: Insured patients — anyone with employer coverage, marketplace insurance, Medicare, or Medicaid — who receive hospital care, especially emergency care, at a hospital or from a hospital-based doctor who is not in their insurance network. Instead of facing unexpected bills for hundreds or thousands of dollars, they would owe only what an in-network provider could charge, unless they knowingly signed a consent form in advance.

how_it_helps.text: Hospitals would have to notify patients on the date of an appointment and again on the date of service whether the hospital or any doctor treating them is outside their insurance network, and if so, estimate the extra amount they would be charged.

For non-emergency out-of-network care, hospitals could charge more than normal in-network cost sharing only if the patient signed a consent document at least 24 hours beforehand, acknowledging the estimated charge and that it does not count toward deductibles or out-of-pocket limits.

For emergency services and same-day care, hospitals and hospital-based providers could not charge the patient more than the cost sharing they would owe an in-network provider, regardless of network status.
The protections applied broadly across coverage types, including group plans, individual market insurance, Medicare, Medicaid, and other government programs.

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals and the out-of-network physicians and staffing companies who work inside them, who would lose the ability to collect balance bills from patients above in-network cost sharing. Hospitals would also bear the cost of setting up notice, estimate, and consent systems to stay eligible for Medicare.

drawbacks.text: The bill did not ban balance billing outright: for scheduled non-emergency care, a hospital could still charge the patient an estimated out-of-network amount after obtaining signed consent 24 hours in advance, and consent forms at hospitals are often signed under stressful conditions.

The bill protected patients but did not resolve the underlying payment dispute between insurers and out-of-network providers — the provider would still face unpaid charges above the patient's share, and critics of this approach argue that capping patient bills without setting an insurer-provider payment standard can push providers to demand higher network rates or pressure hospitals to narrow networks.

Hospitals would have to build and enforce notice, estimate, and consent procedures for nearly every patient as a condition of Medicare participation, a real administrative cost that could fall on smaller critical access hospitals.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients, the benefits are large and direct: surprise bills are among the most common and frustrating medical-billing problems, and the emergency-care cap alone would have eliminated the biggest category of them. The main weaknesses are that the consent carve-out leaves a door open for upcharging on scheduled care, and the bill caps what patients pay without settling what insurers owe providers. On balance, the patient protection outweighs the compliance costs, which are the kind hospitals routinely absorb to remain in Medicare.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to two House committees and a health subcommittee in October 2015, and no committee ever took it up, so it never reached the House floor before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Lloyd Doggett introduced the bill on October 20, 2015, joined by 33 Democratic cosponsors.
The same day, the House referred it to both the Ways and Means Committee and the Energy and Commerce Committee.
Days later it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, and no markup, hearing, committee vote, or floor vote ever followed.
The 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017, with the bill still stalled in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals and out-of-network hospital-based physician practices are better off, because they kept the ability to balance-bill patients above in-network rates for four more years. Insured patients with surprise bills gained nothing from the bill's failure.

for.name: Lloyd Doggett
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited cosponsors

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never held a markup or reported the bill out of committee

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill

sides.party_line_note: All 34 supporters — the sponsor and 33 cosponsors — were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the Republican-led committees that held the bill took no action.

industries.note: Hospitals would lose the ability to bill patients out-of-network rates without prior signed consent, and could not balance-bill emergency patients at all. They would also bear the cost of notice and consent systems to keep their Medicare participation.

industries.industry: Out-of-network hospital-based physician practices (emergency physicians, anesthesiologists, radiologists)
industries.note: These practices collect much of their revenue through balance bills on patients who did not choose them. The bill caps what they could charge patients at in-network cost sharing in emergencies and without 24-hour consent.
The bill leaves insurer payments largely untouched but reduces balance-billing disputes with members. Insurers' interest here runs alongside patients', against out-of-network providers.
